name: Sara Silva

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Sara, thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or any party. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I rear the calves at Oakmere Farm, which the Dunn family run, 400 dairy cows, plus maize and wheat for feed. I've got about 60 calves at any time, so I'm mixing milk, bottle-feeding the new ones, cleaning pens, checking for scours, which is a calf stomach bug. Then afternoons I help wherever, silage, fencing, whatever's needed. I love the calves, every one's got a character, but mucking out pens in the rain gets old.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my partner João in the flat above the old dairy on his parents' farm, about ten minutes away. They've got a small place, 30 cows, potatoes and chickens, and João works there full-time; I help on Saturdays. The rent's low, but the wages are too, and we've got maybe three weeks saved. I've used AI a few times, mostly to help João's mum with the government farm forms, which are a nightmare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's what I expected, a helpful tool for forms but not much else. Farming's about the animals and the weather. I'd say that at church on Sunday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I'm more worried about João's family farm than any AI. Thirty cows doesn't pay any more, and his dad's knees are going. That's the real problem for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the calves at Oakmere and help on the family farm Saturdays. I'd use AI more for the farm forms, it saved João's mum a whole evening last time. And we'd try to save 40 a week toward a deposit on our own place one day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Settled at work, worried at home. That's how it is now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if João's dad can't work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then João does it all, and I'd have to do more too, maybe drop to four days at Oakmere. Thirty cows on João's family farm don't pay any more, and his dad's knees won't last another five winters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned church. Does that matter in how you'd see this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Church is family to us. People help each other at harvest and when someone's sick. That's worth more than any app.

think: João's **family farm** worries her more than AI.
Thirty cows **don't pay** and his dad's knees are going.
do: Keep rearing **calves at Oakmere** and helping on Saturdays.
Use AI more for the **farm forms**.
Save **40 a week** toward a deposit.

fieldNote: Her pressure is the **family farm**, not her own job.
She already uses AI to save **João's mum** an evening of forms.

steps.text: Keep rearing the 60 calves at Oakmere
Use a chatbot for the in-laws' government farm forms
Save 40 a week toward a house deposit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say change is part of farming, we've always adapted. My granddad went from horses to tractors. I'd say be sensible and pick what works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, Mr Dunn has been looking at an automatic calf feeder, and with AI running the herd records, he'd need fewer people. My job could be cut to part-time. The family farm would need me more though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Mr Dunn to let me run the calf feeder if he buys it, so I'm the one he needs. I'd look at whether João's family could buy a second-hand feeder for their calves too. And I'd keep saving, even if it's slow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, honestly. Not panicking, but it's real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell João's parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them small farms need to use the same tools as big ones, or they'll be left behind. My husband-to-be's parents still milk 30 cows in a 1970s parlour, and the Dunn farm down the road is buying robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said husband-to-be. Is there a wedding planned?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not yet, we need the money first. We'd like to marry at our church in a year or two. All this makes me want to wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say families will have to pull together like they did in hard times before. I'd want the government to help farms, not just factories. And I'd pray, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2031 robots could do my calf work, and big robot farms would sell milk so cheap that João's family's 30 cows are finished. That's both our incomes gone in five years. I don't have a plan for that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd cut everything, no car upgrade, no holidays. I'd ask João's parents if we could combine households to save rent, all of us in the farmhouse. And I'd look at whether the family farm could switch to something robots don't do well, like selling eggs and potatoes direct.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, I think. Like when a calf's not breathing and you're rubbing it with straw.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the three-year gap between thinking AI and robots change anything for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For three years the forms and the planning get easy, which helps the family farm. Then the robots come and big farms get even bigger. A computer could fill in João's family's farm forms for free, but a computer can't stop the milk price falling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car I'd been saving for. Then my phone contract. Then we'd stop eating out entirely, which we barely do anyway.

Switch the family farm to **direct sales** of eggs and potatoes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, I'd say there's time if families plan together. Small farms should team up. I'd say that to the other young farmers at church.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With five years, the family farm could change before the robots arrive, maybe more eggs and direct sales. I'd still worry about my job at Oakmere. But we'd have time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd help João's family start selling direct, eggs, potatoes, maybe beef boxes. I'd save 50 a week. And I'd learn the calf feeder systems properly, so I'm worth more to any farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but steady. Like a long lambing, you take it one night at a time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would selling direct help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: People will still want to know where their food comes from. A robot farm can't tell you a story about its hens. People still want to buy eggs from a family they know, and a robot farm can't tell you its hens' names.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned beef boxes. Is João on board?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He's slower than me to change, but he'd come round. His mum's the one who'll push it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is good, I'd say. Time to plan, time to teach the young ones. Nobody should panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be okay. João's family would have time to modernise, and we could take over the farm properly. By then we'd be married with kids, I hope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd marry João in a year or two, at our church. I'd help the family farm save for a robot milker once the price comes down. And keep my job at Oakmere until the family farm can pay us both.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful. A bit nervous, but mostly hopeful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would that family farm look like in 2039?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Robot milker, direct sales, maybe a farm shop. João and me running it, his parents retired in the farmhouse. In 2039 I'd like João and me running his family's farm, with a robot doing the milking and us doing the selling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could still go wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Prices, weather, health. Same as always. But ten years is time to prepare for most things.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because both our incomes are farm incomes and both could go. What would help is government support for small family farms, and loans so they can buy robots too.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about small farms. Big farms will buy the robots first, and small family farms like João's will be left milking the old way until the bank calls.
